subsubtopic: SOUTH AFRICA-CALL FOR ACTION BY COMMONWEALTH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the softly-softly, quietly-quietly, and completely
inappropriately named constructive engagement approach has not worked with South Africa. There can no longer be any doubt that Mr. Botha intends to defend the racist system of apartheid at all costs. The Commonwealth could receive no clearer message than was provided this week with the attacks on Zimbabwe, Zambia, and Botswana, and the promise of further action.
Canada and all Commonwealth countries must act now with strong measures that will leave Mr. Botha with little doubt that freedom-loving people will no longer tolerate his racist regime. If the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) fine words of last October are to mean anything, in the face of Britain's obstinate refusal to act Canada must provide the leadership necessary for the Commonwealth to develop a timely and forceful response, even if without Great Britain.

Mr. Speaker, the difficulty some companies and public sector organizations are having in obtaining liability insurance is by no means unique to Fraser Valley East. Many organizations throughout the country appear to be having similar problems. Possible solutions most frequently mentioned to alleviate these problems are Government actions to limit court awards, to control premium rates, and to enter into the reinsurance or insurance business directly.
Many people look to the federal Government to take action on this serious problem. However, due to constitutional decisions, the role of the federal Government in the regulation of insurance is limited to establishing financial and solvency standards for federally incorporated or registered companies. Matters such as contract provisions, their interpretation, and regulation of premium rates fall under provincial jurisdiction. I urge the federal Government to continue its co-ordinating role in bringing together the provincial Governments in order to deal with this important issue.

May 23, 1986

Mr. Speaker, our farmers have been faced with major problems for many years. However, since the election of our Government, they have regained confidence in the future and they are looking forward to the coming crop year with unprecedented optimism.
They are right to be optimistic as our Government continues to take action to put back the farm sector back on a solid base. This week, the Farm Credit Corporation announced the second reduction of its interest rates in two months.
Farmers in Canada and the Beauce can now benefit from five-year fixed term loans at a rate of 10.75 per cent. For ten-year fixed term loans, the rate has been reduced from 11.5 to 11 per cent. Finally, shared risk mortgage rates have also been reduced.
Mr. Speaker, many Beauce farmers have told me that this Government has done more to help farmers in 20 months than the previous Liberal Government had done in 20 years. We shall continue to work tirelessly for our farmers. The Conservatives view agriculture as a priority in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the Farm Credit Corporation just announced a further reduction in its mortgage rate. For the second time in less than two months these rates have been cut back as a direct result of the Government's economic policies. Under the Commodity-Based Loan Program, the rate on partially indexed loans will be reduced from 8 3/4 per cent to 8 1/2 per cent. On fully indexed loans the rate will remain at 6 per cent. Farm syndicate loans are available at 10.75 per cent instead of 11 per cent.
Earlier this month the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) again confirmed the Government's commitment to agriculture with his announcement on immediate aid to farmers. At the same time we are world leaders in working toward long-term solutions to the international farm crisis. This Government has done more for farmers in 20 months than the previous Government did in 20 years, and we will continue to work for our farmers for many years to come.

Mr. Speaker, tomorrow marks the sixty-eighth anniversary of Canadian women winning the federal vote. This anniversary of women's suffrage is a time to celebrate women's achievements, it is also a time to reflect on the progress our society has made toward the goal of equality between men and women.
There have been some improvements in the status of women and Canadian women are proud of their accomplishments. Women fought for and won the equality provisions in the Charter of Rights. Women have emerged as a driving force in the creation of jobs in the small business sector. Women now occupy positions of influence in the professions and politics.
However, these gains will remain symbolic as long as average Canadian women continue to face inequality in their daily lives. Parliament must pursue the principle and the promise of equality vigorously. There can be no further delay, there must be action for equality now. One challenge that all three Parties must meet is to elect more women to Canadian Legislatures.
May 23, 1986

Mr. Speaker, last Wednesday, the Special Committee on Acid Rain heard the evidence of Mr. Paul Hansen, Environment Canada acid rain advisor who also works for the Isaak Walton League, one of the most respected environmental groups in the United States.
Before the Members of the Committee, Mr. Hansen stated that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) had done a lot to make the issue of acid rain progress politically in the United States. He also added that the battle against acid rain will be won only when American public opinion realizes the seriousness of the problem.
This is why, Mr. Speaker, I ask that, during the coming summer season all Canadians who visit the United States or who receive American tourists tell our southern neighbors about our concerns in this regard and point out that their intervention is essential if we want to win this fight and improve the quality of life for the citizens of both countries.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Bank of Canada announced another reduction in its bank rate. Today the rate fell by 16 basis points and is now fixed at 8.43 per cent. This represents a drop of nearly 4 per cent since the election of our Government roughly 20 months ago.
Events are now unfolding as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) said they would. Interest rates are down, unemployment is down, the dollar is strengthening, and the economic outlook for Canada has not been this good in years. Yesterday's further drop in interest rates will be welcomed by the business community, by consumers, and by Governments, all of whom have seen their borrowing costs reduced dramatically since the election of our Government in September, 1984.
The Opposition doomsters and gloomsters can holler and criticize to their hearts' content. The Canadian public has shown more sense and has chosen to participate in this recovery rather than wallow in criticism and faultfinding, as do the Liberals and the NDP.

Mr. Speaker, in Ottawa this Sunday, under the aegis of UNICEF, a special run will take place. A Race Against Time/Sport Aid will raise money which will go to organizations involved in African relief. I hope Members of this House will agree to sponsor one of the many runners and will pledge some money here on the Hill. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this situation is utterly ridiculous. At the very beginning of trade talks with the United States, the Prime Minister's friend, President Reagan, by his own act and his own hand, imposes a 35 per cent tariff on cedar shakes and shingles from Canada. This is putting $250 million worth of exports and perhaps thousands of jobs in British Columbia in jeopardy. Will the Prime Minister tell us, in view of his relationship, whether he had advance notice of this action by the President and, if so, what steps were taken to head it off? If he did not, how can that be explained?

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Associate Minister of National Defence. On January 27 the Secretary of State for External Affairs wrote a letter stating the following:
Canada's first priority in relation to chemical weapons continues to be to pursue actively at the Conference on Disarmament (CD) in Geneva the conclusion of a complete and verifiable ban on all chemical weapons.

May 23, 1986

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Associate Minister of National Defence):
subsubtopic: U.S. PLAN TO RESUME PRODUCTION OF CHEMICAL WEAPONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the position of this Government on chemical weapons is exactly the same as the position of the previous Government. We fully endorse the position taken in 1970 that Canada will not have chemical weapons, will not use chemical weapons, will not produce them, and will not keep them in store. That remains our position. We adopted that position after the position adopted in 1969 by the United States unilaterally to stop the production of new chemical weapons. In the meantime the Soviets continued with production and have built up their chemical capabilities.
In order to maintain the deterrence which is what NATO is all about-to avoid war-it is deemed prudent by all NATO countries that the U.S. increase or modernize its chemical capability for the maintenance of that deterrence and peace. There is no inconsistency at all. We are carrying on the policies of the previous Government which were endorsed by the Hon. Member.

Mr. Speaker, Canada is a party to the 1925 Geneva Protocol banning the use of chemical weapons. That was a policy of the previous Government as well. Since the Government has failed to bring forward a White Paper on defence policy, will the Associate Minister of National Defence commit himself and the Government to a debate in the House on such major international issues as this one so that Canadians may learn what is going on?
